claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings develop nanoscale oxide layers during high-temperature wear.
The high-temperature oxide layers are continuous and adherent.
The oxide layers are enriched primarily in Cr and Cu.
The oxide layers mediate deformation and inhibit crack propagation.
Formation of the oxide layers enhances the coating's wear resistance.
The as-deposited coating has a homogeneous, unoxidized microstructure.
Protective nanoscale oxides form both at the coating surface and along grain boundaries.
The oxide layers maintain adhesion to the underlying metal.
High temperature accelerates oxygen diffusion into the coating.
Accelerated oxygen diffusion produces stable oxides in situ that passivate the surface.
The oxides impede dislocation motion and local shear deformation.
Impeded dislocation motion and local shear reduce plastic deformation and suppress microcrack initiation.
Reduced plastic deformation and microcrack initiation lower the overall wear rate.
At approximately 600°C and a moderate load such as 2 N, oxidation is significant while the alloy and substrate remain below their melting points.
High-temperature oxidizing wear will produce a lower wear rate than room-temperature or inert-atmosphere baseline testing.
Improved mechanical integrity will correlate with continuous, adherent surface oxide layers.
The beneficial effect is expected near 600°C under moderate wear loads.
At more extreme temperatures, coating melting or oxide spallation may eliminate the predicted benefit.

contradictions.description: The primary comparison is inconsistently defined: some fields compare 600°C oxidizing wear with room-temperature or inert testing, whereas the falsification experiment compares oxidizing and inert atmospheres at the same high temperature. The former confounds temperature with atmosphere, while the latter isolates oxidation.
